Consider the circle of radius $10$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ that traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(10,0).$

$x=$
{{field-1}}$,\,y=$
{{field-2}}$,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi )$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius is $r=10.$ Substituting $r=10$ gives

$$
x=10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=10\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14039602/assets/d50e70570bbf054d8ab0bda89ce09e3bec855af2a0ef94d2fcf1a8aea103b53c.png)

The semi-circle above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a semi-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14039602/assets/9f515c8b70ee6902df4c694f7d7b50efb4ff54d24b0cb25b9173d439fea84210.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\pi ]$, we get the required semi-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the semi-circle are 

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,\pi ].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
questions.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{(x+1)}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}(y+2) & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{(y+2)}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{(x+1)}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}{(y+2)}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 4{(x+1)}^{2}+4{(y+2)}^{2} & =9 \\ {(x+1)}^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation of the circle is ${(x+1)}^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2}=\frac{9}{4}.$

questions.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2},\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-\frac{1}{2}) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{5}(x-\frac{1}{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+\frac{1}{2}) & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{5}(y+\frac{1}{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=25.$

questions.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =9({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =9(1) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$

questions.problem:
The Cartesian equation of the circle defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -5,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +13,\,0\le \theta <2\pi 
$$

is given by

$(x\,+$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}+(y\,-$
{{field-2}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{(x+5)}^{2}}{49} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-13 & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-13)^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{(y-13)}^{2}}{49} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(x+5)}^{2}}{49}+\frac{{(y-13)}^{2}}{49} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{(x+5)}^{2}}{49}+\frac{{(y-13)}^{2}}{49} & =1 \\ {(x+5)}^{2}+{(y-13)}^{2} & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation is ${(x+5)}^{2}+{(y-13)}^{2}=49.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown below. Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ that traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(2,0).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14039602/assets/156d160267551e9dbf4db42b14b1e0dbb46ab658a836a760cf31a42eb89662d3.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$ centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius is $r = 2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=2\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
canonical_examples.problem: Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ that generates a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(4,6).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x= r\cos\theta+a,\quad y=r\sin\theta+b,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(4,6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\cos\theta+4,\quad y=2\sin\theta+6,\quad\theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14039602/assets/f44fad12ad1f7d465423f92258caae38e0c536153ba2c3c3a6de573061c69993.png)

The quarter-circle above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x = 6\cos\theta, \qquad y = 6\sin\theta.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, the radius $r = 6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14039602/assets/4bd384e2b1a9d0568617ddbfd5ac7dbe9630882b45c40d7912f4809a6e0be551.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta$ to $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right],$ we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\cos\theta + 2,\quad y=3\sin\theta - 4, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+4}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-2)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 9.$
